meta.title: SRO conversion claim graph, Downtown Eastside Vancouver
meta.unit: A domino is an edge: a sourced claim that one decision option or outcome moves another outcome, with a direction and a lag in years.

rules.direction: + raises the outcome, - lowers it, 0 holds it steady
rules.lag: years after the decision takes effect; effect lands at t + lag_min and persists through lag_max
rules.evidence: applies to observation edges only. strong = peer-reviewed quantitative; moderate = peer-reviewed qualitative, or an official longitudinal data series; weak = thesis, advocacy survey, or a one-off government statement. Null on mechanism and theory edges.
rules.geography: vancouver = DTES or Vancouver evidence; other = evidence from elsewhere, transferability not shown
rules.fork: edges sharing a fork id contradict each other and must both be shown
rules.stop: a decision option with zero outgoing edges halts the run and asks for a source
rules.claim_type: mechanism = follows from how the policy or arithmetic is defined, no evidence grade; observation = an empirical study measured it; theory = a peer-reviewed argument not measured in this case

decisions.label: SRA conversion or demolition permit
decisions.who: City of Vancouver, under the SRA Bylaw
decisions.note: minor_repair_staff: since 2015, repairs that relocate a tenant but keep the room in the bylaw are approved by the Chief Housing Officer without Council. Most renovation cases take this route.

decisions.label: Minimum unit size in square feet
decisions.note: 200 sf is the live threshold in current permit reports: a renovated building whose average unit is under 200 sf stays designated under the SRA By-law; over 200 sf it is removed and secured as social housing instead. Mechanism edges now exist for 200. No observation edge on tenant outcomes by unit size; that stop remains.

decisions.label: Rent rule when a room turns over
Social to market mix in new buildings
Per-room charge for removing a room from the bylaw
decisions.note: Charge history: $5,000 (2003), $15,000, $125,000 (2015), $230,000 (2020), $300,000 (2023). Last actually charged in 2015; since then waived for housing agreements or set by pro forma (Clifton 2025, $1.1M for 74 rooms).

outcomes.label: Tenant mortality risk
outcomes.baseline: SRO tenants already carry a standardized mortality ratio of 4.83 (2013 cohort) to 8.43 (2017 cohort), with near-universal substance dependence and high rates of psychosis, HIV and hepatitis C. Any forced move acts on this baseline.

outcomes.label: Replacement rooms occupied
outcomes.note: No sourced edge into this outcome yet. The lag from fee to occupied replacement room is unknown. Source needed: Council reports on reserve fund spending. Until then the tool stops here.

outcomes.label: Tenants who return after works
outcomes.note: No sourced edge into this outcome. The City requires a relocation plan but does not publish return rates. Second honest stop beside unit_size_sf=200.

outcomes.label: Building stays under the SRA By-law
Rooms secured by a housing agreement

edges.note: Policy mechanism, not a study. The bylaw exists because conversions remove rooms.
Inference: typical SRA room is about 100 sf, so a 250 sf unit merges rooms. Guideline says it aims to minimize unit loss.
320 sf is the SRA threshold; above it a unit leaves the bylaw's definition.
Arithmetic from the option, not a finding.
General population, UK panel data. Effect partly relative to peers, not absolute.
Fewer units means fewer tenants can return after renovation. Direction is negative because the edge reads: units down, evictions up.
Honer finds illness-specific care has little effect on multimorbidity; disruption of that care on a high-SMR baseline is the inferred link.
Partial replacement frees floor area for market rental under the 60/40 rule. Needs an observation edge showing conversions actually produced market units; source hunt pending.
100 new units lead 45 to 70 people out of below-median tracts within five years. US cities; chains below the SRO tier not observed.
5 to 7 percent relative rent decline near large new buildings in low-income areas.
Rival to e12. Investment signals closing of the rent gap and draws further capital.
Burnett shows the DTES rent gap closing through commercial and consumption change first.
Concentrated non-market stock is one of Ley and Dobson's impediments.
Social mix as state-led gentrification. Theory, UK and US cases.
MSW thesis, qualitative, three years after the LAP.
Ties persisted despite mix. Rival to e21.
Montreal. Mix can build cross-class ties under some conditions.
Official biennial series, not peer reviewed. The 21 percent rise is between tenancies, which is the mechanism vacancy control targets. Peer-reviewed analysis of the series not found; keep looking.
Official biennial series, not peer reviewed. The 21 percent rise is between tenancies, which is the mechanism vacancy control targets. Peer-reviewed analysis of the series not found; keep looking.
Relocation during repair is the eviction pathway Fleming describes. Confirm the paper covers staff-route relocations specifically.
Bylaw directs the charge into a reserve earmarked for replacement housing.
Policy-learning edge: each fee increase followed survey evidence of room loss. Direction negative because rooms down, fee up. Official record, not a study.
Average over 200 sf removes the building from the bylaw; under 200 sf keeps it. Regent and Thornton removed, Keefer retained.
Self-contained units averaging over 200 sf cut unit count to about half: 161 to 77, 23 to 12. Official permit records, two buildings.

In six of seven permit files tenants were already gone before the application, by closure order, fire, or owner relocation. The permit does not cause the move; it follows it. Negative lag is deliberate.
The fee has not been charged at its listed rate since 2015. Reserve inflow from fees is near zero in practice; e25 describes the rule, this describes the record.
The bylaw directs the charge into the replacement reserve (e25). A building whose fee is waived pays nothing in, so the reserve does not move for that building.

One case only: Low Young Court (2015), fee waived in exchange for a 30-year housing agreement on 8 of 12 rooms. The bar runs the 30-year term of that agreement. One case is not a pattern; more waivers are needed before this is a claim about the fee.
